case_prompt: A 77-year-old woman presented with 2 weeks of progressively worsening oral tongue pain, ulceration, and odynophagia leading to dehydration. She reported that her tongue turned blue before ulceration. She denied fevers, chills, malaise, scalp or jaw tenderness, headaches, or vision changes. Initial outpatient treatment with trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole, then amoxicillin–clavulanate, followed by acyclovir and fluconazole, did not improve her symptoms. On examination, she had dry mucous membranes and a well-demarcated area of necrosis involving the anterior one-third to one-half of the tongue, which was tender to palpation. Laboratory testing showed a leukocyte count of 22 000/µL, a platelet count of 716 000/µL, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 65 mm/h. A CT angiogram of the head and neck revealed an undulated-beaded appearance of the distal internal carotid arteries and vertebral arteries bilaterally. A biopsy of the tongue demonstrated marked acute inflammation and granulation tissue with focal loss of the squamous mucosa; staining showed no fungal elements, and immunohistochemistry showed no cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, or varicella zoster virus.

She reported that her tongue turned blue before ulceration.
She denied fevers, chills, malaise, scalp or jaw tenderness, headaches, or vision changes.

Laboratory testing showed a leukocyte count of 22 000/µL, a platelet count of 716 000/µL, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 65 mm/h.
A CT angiogram of the head and neck revealed an undulated-beaded appearance of the distal internal carotid arteries and vertebral arteries bilaterally.

A biopsy of the tongue demonstrated marked acute inflammation and granulation tissue with focal loss of the squamous mucosa; staining showed no fungal elements, and immunohistochemistry showed no cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, or varicella zoster virus.

diagnostic_reasoning: 1. Infectious causes were excluded—“No fungal elements were identified with staining, and no viruses…were identified with immunohistochemistry markers.” 2. Diffuse atherosclerosis was less likely—“the undulated-beaded appearance of the distal internal carotid and vertebral arteries bilaterally was more consistent with skip lesions occurring secondary to a vasculitic process than diffuse atherosclerosis.” 3. Other vasculitides were considered—“differential for tongue necrosis includes…other vasculitides such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis or polyarteritis nodosa.” 4. Giant cell arteritis was favored given epidemiology and rarity of lingual necrosis—“GCA is likely the most common cause of lingual necrosis when it does present.”

selection.screen_reason: Tongue necrosis in an elderly woman with high ESR, thrombocytosis and beaded carotid and vertebral arteries, with infection excluded on biopsy, points to giant cell arteritis.
selection.second_look_note: Tongue pain with blue discoloration before ulceration and failed antimicrobials frame ischemic necrosis that inflammatory markers and beaded arteries on CT angiography decide.
